scenes.heading: Aromatic compounds
scenes.sub: Why benzene swaps instead of adds
scenes.say: Aspirin, polystyrene and many dyes all contain a benzene ring. Aromatic rings are unusually stable, and that one fact controls how chemists build almost every aromatic drug.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: One group chat where all six friends see every message
scenes.science: Six π electrons delocalised over all six carbons
scenes.breaks: a group chat has messages going back and forth, but benzene never switches between structures. It's one hybrid all the time.
scenes.say: The old picture of benzene, with three double bonds, is like three private chats. Real benzene is one group chat. All six pi electrons are shared over all six carbons. So every carbon–carbon bond is the same length, about one hundred and thirty-nine picometres, and the ring is extra stable.
scenes.caption: The old picture of benzene, with three double bonds, is like three private chats. Real benzene is one group chat. All six π electrons are shared over all six carbons. So every C–C bond is the same length, about 139 pm, and the ring is extra stable.

scenes.heading: Is it aromatic? CPFC
scenes.say: To be aromatic, tick all four: cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and a count of four n plus two pi electrons. Six is sweet, four is foul. A planar, conjugated ring with four or eight pi electrons is antiaromatic and very unstable.
scenes.caption: To be aromatic, tick all four: Cyclic, Planar, Fully conjugated, and a Count of 4n + 2 π electrons. Six is sweet, four is foul. A planar, conjugated ring with 4 or 8 π electrons is antiaromatic and very unstable.

scenes.heading: Electrophilic aromatic substitution
scenes.say: Benzene keeps its ring by swapping, like a footy interchange. First, a catalyst makes a strong electrophile. The ring attacks it, forming an arenium ion. That's the slow step. Then a base removes H plus, and the aromatic ring is restored.
scenes.caption: Benzene keeps its ring by swapping, like a footy interchange. First, a catalyst makes a strong electrophile. The ring attacks it, forming an arenium ion. That's the slow step. Then a base removes H⁺, and the aromatic ring is restored.

scenes.heading: Directing groups

left.title: Ortho/para directors
points: Lone pair or alkyl on the ring

right.title: Meta directors
points: δ+ atom bonded to the ring

scenes.say: Lone pair? Ortho para there. Groups like O H share a lone pair that stabilises the positive charge, so they direct ortho and para. Electron-withdrawing groups like nitro drain the charge, so they direct meta. Halogens are awkward: they deactivate the ring but still direct ortho and para.
scenes.caption: Lone pair? Ortho/para there. Groups like –OH share a lone pair that stabilises the positive charge, so they direct ortho and para. Electron-withdrawing groups like –NO₂ drain the charge, so they direct meta. Halogens are awkward: they deactivate the ring but still direct ortho/para.

scenes.heading: Worked example: order matters
scenes.question: From benzene, make 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene.
lines: The groups are meta to each other
–NO₂ is a meta director: add it first
scenes.say: The two groups are meta to each other, so the meta director goes on first. Nitrate benzene, then brominate. The nitro group sends bromine to the meta position. If you wanted the para product, you'd brominate first. The order of steps decides the pattern.

points: Six delocalised π electrons, all bonds equal
Acylation: no rearrangement, stops at one
scenes.say: Quick recap. Benzene's six pi electrons are delocalised. Aromatic means cyclic, planar, conjugated, with four n plus two electrons. Benzene substitutes rather than adds. And the order of steps sets the pattern. Now try the practice questions!
